An ant starts crawling from one end of a 1 km rubber band at a constant 1 cm/s. At the end of every second, the entire band is instantly and uniformly stretched by another 1 km. Does the ant ever reach the far end?
choices: Yes — the ant's fractional progress each second forms a divergent harmonic series, so it eventually covers the whole band
No — the ant can only reach the end once the stretching stops
It depends on exactly where on the band the ant starts

questions.q: A class takes a test. The students who scored in the top 10% are given a harder retest the next day, and on average they score lower the second time. A teacher concludes the harder test caused the drop. Is that conclusion justified?
choices: No — this is regression to the mean: unusually high scores tend to be followed by scores closer to average even without any real change
No, because test scores are entirely random and carry no information
Yes — the second test was objectively harder, so it must have caused the lower scores
Yes, but only because the grading got stricter overnight

questions.q: You paid $50, non-refundable, for tonight's concert ticket, but you've come down with a cold and won't enjoy the show. Rationally, should the $50 you already spent affect whether you go?
choices: Yes — go, but only to demand a partial refund at the door
No — it's a sunk cost that's gone either way; only tonight's expected enjoyment should matter
No — skip it, since paid tickets are always bad value
Yes — you should go anyway, or the $50 is wasted

questions.q: During WWII, statistician Abraham Wald studied bullet-hole patterns on bombers that returned from missions: the wings and fuselage were riddled with holes, while the engines and cockpit were almost untouched. Where did he recommend adding armor?
choices: Spread the armor evenly across the whole aircraft
The wings and fuselage, since that's clearly where planes take the most hits
Nowhere — the data shows these bombers were rarely hit at all
The engines and cockpit — planes hit there rarely made it back to be counted
